profile.technology: ABILITY is developing a fully implantable brain-computer interface that sits under the scalp and uses high-density ECoG electrodes on the brain surface to record neural activity. Instead of a battery-powered transmitter, its proprietary laser-based optical data link sends the complete raw neural signal wirelessly through intact skin. Adaptive AI decodes these signals into speech and, later, movement, with the company controlling the implant, algorithm and app.

products.description: A fully implantable, ECoG-based device placed entirely under the scalp to record brain signals.

products.name: System
products.description: An end-to-end speech neuroprosthesis platform that transmits neural data through the skin and decodes it into speech.

conditions: Paralysis (movement restoration planned as a future application)
milestones: March 2025: spun out from the Wyss Center in Geneva as an independent company, ABILITY Neurotech.
May 2026: received IMDD approval from the Dutch ethics committee NedMec for a first chronic implantation study in ALS patients at UMC Utrecht.
July 2026: announced first-in-human procedure at TUM University Hospital Rechts der Isar in Munich.
Chronic First-in-Human implantation planned for Q4 2026 with TU Graz (Austria) and UMC Utrecht (Netherlands).

profile.technology: Axoft is developing a bioinspired implantable neural interface whose soft material mimics the soft tissues of the brain, which the company says improves biocompatibility, signal quality and stability over time. The implant is bidirectional: an integrated circuit processes the neural data it records and sends it to software, and that software can send commands back to stimulate the brain electrically. The probes are designed to pass through a 2 mm burr hole using standard neuronavigation tools, and Axoft is building its own Brain Foundation Model software to decode neural signals.

products.description: A soft, bioinspired neural probe with ultra-high electrode density, designed for long-term bidirectional communication with any brain region at single-neuron resolution.

products.name: Brain Foundation Model
products.description: Axoft's in-development AI software for decoding and interpreting neural signals from the implant, intended to improve over time.

profile.technology: Axorus uses genetics-free photoacoustic neuromodulation. Smart glasses with a near-infrared laser project light patterns onto a pigmented contact lens. The lens material converts that light into highly localized ultrasound waves through the photoacoustic effect, and these waves are meant to stimulate retinal neurons to recreate visual perception. The company describes this as a fully non-invasive, reversible approach, with preclinical in vivo evidence of retinal and visual-cortex activation.

products.description: A pigmented contact lens worn daily like a regular lens, intended to restore sight for people with damaged retinas; still in preclinical development.

products.name: Laser projector glasses
products.description: Smart glasses with a near-infrared laser emitter that project light patterns onto the contact lens to trigger the photoacoustic effect.

milestones: Preclinical trials underway at the Institut de la Vision in Paris, France
Preclinical in vivo proof of non-invasive photoacoustic activation of the retina and visual areas of the brain
Published 'A flexible photoacoustic retinal prosthesis' in Nature Communications (2025)
Since May 2025, company focused exclusively on the photoacoustic contact lens after discontinuing implant technologies

profile.technology: BIOS describes its Universal Neural Interface as a connection made directly to the peripheral nervous system, the nerves running from the spinal cord out to the limbs. The site says this link lets the brain communicate with robotic limbs or digital devices in a seamless, intuitive way. Per the site, the system supports closed-loop control of movement together with sensory feedback.

profile.technology: Blackrock's brain-computer interface hardware uses small electrode arrays, such as the Utah Array, that are placed in or on the brain to pick up neural signals. Software decodes those signals into intended actions, which can drive robotic arms, cursors, or communication tools. Some systems also deliver electrical stimulation back to the brain to produce sensations such as touch or artificial vision.

profile.technology: CorTec builds fully implantable systems that communicate directly with the nervous system. Its Brain Interchange device is a closed-loop, bidirectional brain-computer interface, meaning it can both read neural activity and deliver stimulation back to the brain based on what it detects. The company also offers its implant technology (electrodes, electronics, software, packaging and integration) to other developers through its CDMO service.

profile.technology: Corticale builds minimally invasive, CMOS-based neural implants that sit within brain tissue. Each probe carries 1024 independent recording sensors spaced 30 micrometers apart, and each sensor is smaller than a neuron. Together they capture both single-cell action potentials and local field potentials, giving high-resolution readouts from hundreds of cells across the depth of the tissue.

profile.technology: Epia's system pairs a proprietary implant that sits under the skin in the skull, without piercing the dura, with a brain interface that learns a person's intent and how they express it. Adaptive AI models interpret the scene and the objects in it and select the movement needed. A lightweight soft-robotics hand exoskeleton (glove) then carries out the grasp or release, and the implant is recharged wirelessly through a headset.

profile.technology: Morph uses non-invasive EEG (electroencephalography) sensors placed on the head to capture cortical signals that reflect a person's motor intent. Adaptive models then decode that intent and learn each user over time. The decoded commands are translated into precise motion for compatible devices, such as prosthetic hands, without surgery or muscle-based control.

profile.technology: Neurosoft builds soft, elastic brain interfaces that the site says are 1000 to 100,000 times softer and 3 to 5 times thinner than alternatives, so they mechanically match neural tissue more closely. The company says these interfaces can be folded and unfolded into extreme form factors, reach into brain sulci, and be implanted minimally invasively. On the software side, the company uses artificial intelligence to analyse brain recordings for biomarker detection, optimise neuromodulation, and decode motor and speech intentions.

profile.technology: NeuroXess develops implantable flexible brain-computer interfaces that sit in or on the brain and read neural signals. Its in-house hardware chips and AI decoding algorithms translate a patient's motor and speech intent into cursor movements and synthesized Mandarin speech, with a full-link latency the company puts at under 50 ms. The company's XessOS BCI operating system then lets patients control computers, browse the web, operate smart home devices and use AI assistants by thought.

profile.technology: Phosphoenix's approach uses a neuroprosthesis that electrically stimulates the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a deep relay in the brain's visual pathway, bypassing damaged eyes. By coordinating many electrodes, the system evokes localized visual percepts (phosphenes) that combine into structured spatial patterns to support basic functional vision such as navigation and obstacle detection.

profile.technology: StairMed develops an invasive brain-computer interface built around an ultra-flexible micro-nano electrode, about 1 μm thick, whose mechanical properties are said to be similar to brain tissue. The implant is housed in titanium alloy or zirconia ceramic, and its brain control software supports training protocols that aim to restore motor ability.

profile.technology: Subsense's NanoBCI combines two types of biocompatible nanoparticles placed in the brain with a wearable headset. The nanoparticles are introduced intranasally and are described as navigating in a controlled way to target brain regions, where they act as antennas to read and write neural signals. The wearable hardware wirelessly connects to and controls the nanoparticles, aiming to provide a non-surgical, bidirectional brain-computer interface.

profile.technology: Synaptrix builds non-invasive brain-computer interfaces by combining EEG hardware, large neural datasets, and deep learning models designed for brain signals. Its software models try to reconstruct high-resolution neural activity from scalp EEG recordings, aiming to recover more information than conventional EEG captures. The company's stated goal is to close the gap between non-invasive systems and implants, with the aim of controlling devices such as a powered wheelchair from brain signals.

profile.technology: Imeka's ANDI software works on diffusion-based white matter MRI, a standard type of MRI scan that measures the microstructure of the brain's nerve fiber tracts. The software combines this imaging with artificial intelligence to analyze the white matter in detail. It turns raw scan data into a fully automated, quantitative report on white matter health, including neuroinflammation, axonal integrity, and myelin integrity. The site says data can be collected in as little as five minutes on a standard MRI machine.

profile.technology: optohive's HiveOne uses functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which shines safe near-infrared light into the scalp and measures changes in blood oxygenation that reflect brain activity. Proprietary silicon photomultiplier sensors, developed at ETH Zurich, detect the light, short channels built into each optode help remove scalp contribution, and an AI-supported software pipeline turns the raw signals into structured data.

profile.technology: The system uses a smart neurostimulator implanted near the sacral nerve to deliver sacral neuromodulation therapy for urinary urge incontinence. Unlike traditional implants, the device has no implanted battery; power is supplied through a discreet external battery worn daily. That external battery charges wirelessly, like a smartphone, which avoids the complications associated with implanted batteries. The company's core power-transfer approach, which it calls "mid field" technology, is what allows the implant to receive power and communicate without wires.

profile.technology: αDBS is an adaptive deep brain stimulation system that records brain signals (the α/β spectrum) from the implant about every 10 minutes. A patented proportional control algorithm uses those readings to adjust stimulation automatically, aiming to keep the patient within their therapeutic window instead of delivering a fixed signal. Brain data is also stored on the WebBioBank cloud platform, where physicians can review it and optimize therapy over time.

profile.technology: SonoCloud® is an intracranial implant that emits low-intensity pulsed ultrasound into the brain. Gas microbubbles infused alongside the ultrasound oscillate under its pulses, which temporarily and reversibly opens the blood-brain barrier for several hours. Drugs given close to the sonication session can then reach brain tissue in higher concentrations.

products.name: SonoCloud®
products.description: Intracranial implant that uses low-intensity pulsed ultrasound to temporarily open the blood-brain barrier so chemotherapy or other therapeutic agents can reach the brain.

profile.technology: Clee Medical is developing an imaging and sensing technology meant to give surgeons real-time, ultra-high-resolution views of the brain during an operation, without contrast agents or radiation. It is delivered through a disposable endoscopic probe that works alongside existing neurosurgical equipment, with machine learning and AI providing real-time guidance. The company describes it as filling the intraoperative imaging gap left by pre-operative MRI, which it says is often insufficient for precise targeting.

profile.technology: Coapt's system reads the tiny electrical signals (myoelectricity) that residual muscles produce on the skin, using an array of surface electrodes that cover the area of the underlying muscle contractions. Machine-learning algorithms decode these repeatable patterns in real time to work out which arm or hand movement the user intends. The system then tells the prosthesis to perform that movement, allowing control of multiple prosthetic functions.

profile.technology: Cogitat builds deep learning models that read EEG brainwave signals and translate them into digital commands, such as attention or movement control. The decoders are person-independent, so they can work on new users without long calibration sessions, and they are designed to run on any EEG headset or sensor configuration. The company also states that they tolerate real-world signal problems such as poor skin-sensor contact or sensor hardware failures. Its NeuroRVQ approach turns raw biosignals into compact tokens for small, efficient foundation models.

profile.technology: NeuroPASS is a skull-embedded implant designed to sit beneath the scalp in the temporal region, using space that the company says is otherwise unused. It is meant to give a repeatable route for delivering drugs directly to the brain, bypassing the blood-brain barrier that blocks most systemic drugs. The company reports that convective drug delivery across the brain was demonstrated preclinically with NeuroPASS, and the design is MRI-Conditional and modular across indications.

profile.technology: Nimbus runs its software engine on RxInfer, a reactive message-passing framework for Bayesian inference, and it can freeze a large pretrained EEG encoder while adapting a small calibrated Bayesian head to a new user. The Bayesian model reports calibrated uncertainty, which lets the system suppress unreliable outputs such as those caused by blinks or noise.

products.name: Zeta TMS Robotic System (Zeta TMS Navigation System)
products.description: Navigated, robotic system for transcranial magnetic stimulation that the site says has FDA 510(k) clearance.

conditions: Major Depressive Disorder and other neurological conditions
milestones: Jul 2026: Zeta TMS Robotic System received FDA 510(k) clearance (K261471), classified as a Class II stereotaxic instrument
Jun 2026: First patient treated with the FDA-cleared Zeta TMS Navigation System at a HOPE Therapeutics clinic in Sarasota
Oct 2026: Announced collaboration with DARPA in support of the Phase 3 SPARC-TMS clinical study
Breakthrough clinical study in bedside external ventricular drain cases reported on the site
